benchmark_kind: growth law of the oblivious sort-join used by the volume-hiding descriptor remap
protocol: MP-SPDZ Semi, three local parties. Threat model unchanged: any two of three servers may collude.
scope_warning: radix_sort measured at 1024/2048/4096 rows with 20-bit keys and a 2-column payload, on a single host. MetaQA-scale figures remain EXTRAPOLATIONS, now 144x beyond the largest measured point rather than the 575x of the previous estimate. Passive protocol only.
why_this_was_measured: The descriptor remap is 98% of the cost of owner-blind pooling, and its estimate rested on a single measurement at 1024 rows with 16-bit keys, extrapolated under an assumed LINEAR growth law. Both the width and the law were wrong.

what_the_data_shows.cost_per_row_is_not_constant: 59.51 -> 63.99 -> 68.47 MB/row across the measured range, so the linear law used previously understates growth.
what_the_data_shows.mechanism: radix_sort runs one shuffle-based pass per key bit, and each pass is itself super-linear, so n*log(n) is the expected shape and is what the data supports.
what_the_data_shows.key_width_correction: The earlier figure used 16-bit keys. The remap sorts by directory row, needing log2(389115) = 19-20 bits. Cost scales close to linearly in key width: 52,000.7 MB at 16 bits versus 60,935.7 MB at 20 bits for the same 1024 rows, a 1.17x increase for a 1.25x width increase.

corrected_projection.reported_value: the n*log(n) figure, since it is the better fit and the pessimistic end

impact_on_volume_hiding.verdict: Still viable, and still far better than uniform padding for any federation with unequal participants, but materially more expensive than first estimated. A unit test asserting the old 15% bound failed on the corrected model, which is how the change surfaced.

what_this_does_not_show: Any measurement at or near 589,479 records; the projection still extrapolates 144x.
Any implementation of the remap; only the sort primitive it would use was measured.
Any real dataset, WAN, or multi-host result.
That n*log(n) continues to hold two orders of magnitude beyond the measured range.
